content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper proposes an 8-bit quantization method to quantize the Transformer, which is a popular machine translation model. Uniform min-max quantization is used for computational expensive operations during the inference. The authors also propose to bucket the weights before quantization to reduce quantization error. Experiments are performed on WMT translation tasks.

The paper is overall easy to follow. One of my main concerns is about the novelty since both the min-max quantization and bucketing the weights before quantization are not new. Another concern is that one important goal of quantization is to speed up inference, however, no inference time is reported in the paper. Can the authors provide the inference time results on some typical cpu/gpus?

From Table 4, the proposed quantization has much larger BLEU gain than the base transformer after 100k training steps, than that after full training (Table 2). Does this mean the proposed quantization converges slower at the later stage of training? How many training steps are run to reach the result of the proposed method in Table 1? Can the authors compare the training curve of the base transformer and the quantized one?

From Table 4, the earlier the quantization starts, the better the final performance. What about the performance of training from scratch? Will this give better performance?

------------post rebuttal comment-----------
I thank the authors for their detailed response. However, the concerns on the novelty of the quantization technique and the inference efficiency of the proposed method still remain. Thus I keep my score unchanged.
-------------------------------------------------------

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments.
As for your concerns:

The following concern is similar to one of Reviewer #3’s and so we share with you the same comment:
Contrary to what you have mentioned, the main idea of this paper is not uniform quantization and bucketing, it’s about quantization improving or not worsening translation quality. This is an important distinction as it is what we believe make this work novel. The Transformer paper is already two years old. If quantizing the architecture without impairing results was an easy task, papers would of had come out by then. The few papers released so far quantize much fewer components than we do and none of the proposed methods who quantize activations have managed to keep performance on par with full-precision. Considering all of this, we believe our work to be novel and impactful to the community.

About your comment on inference time, we also share a similar comment that we gave to Reviewer #2:
We strongly believe that inference time is a terrible metric for comparing methods, as this is highly hardware and implementation dependent. Reporting results such as: “our method performed X time faster than full-precision” is meaningless. Someone trying to replicate this could end up with completely different time gains. Take half-precision on Volta GPUs as an example. Reports of inference speed gains for using half-precision vary wildly. Hopefully you will agree on this.

We have added details about the number of training steps for Table 1 in the paper. With regards to training curves, we did take a look at them and saw no significant difference or any distinct pattern. They are almost exactly the same. We added a mention about this in the paper.

About the following comment: “From Table 4, the proposed quantization has much larger BLEU gain than the base transformer after 100k training steps, than that after full training (Table 2)”
We believe you mean: “after full training (Table 1)” since in Table 2, all base models are trained for 100k steps. We believe that the difference in BLEU is only more significant for the EN-FR task. We do not believe and have not observed a difference in convergence. We think the difference in results in Table 1 is solely due to training time. The original Transformer paper does not provide the number of training steps for these results.

For you question about training from scratch a Transformer with quantization, we’ve clarified this in the paper. We consider training with quantization from step 100 to be “from scratch” as we need at least a few steps to compute the running estimates.

Again, thank you for your comments. In spite of the disagreements, your comments did help us improve our paper. We are grateful to you for such and hope our clarifications and changes will entice you to review your score.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
This paper proposes a method for reducing the required memory space by a quantization technique.
This paper specifically focuses on reducing it for the Transformer architecture. 
Several similar methods that shared the same motivation have already been proposed in the literature.
Moreover, the main idea of the proposed method is the uniform quantization method, which has described in the previous study.
Therefore, unfortunately, the technical novelty seems to be very marginal and narrow.
It is hard to say that this paper is innovative or has enough contribution and influence on the community.
Please clearly elaborate if the authors think that the proposed method has certain technical novelty, and I missed to recognize it.


1,
However, I am a bit surprised by the results of the proposed method; it successfully achieved the on-par result (or even improving) to the standard (non-quantized) models on the well-studied WMT14 EN-FR and WMT14 EN-DE translation tasks.
According to Tables 1 and 2, it reduced the required memory space 1/4 from the original while maintaining any performance degradation, or even it slightly improves the performance.
It is good to see such a simple approach offers a better result.
I think that the experimental results may offer a new insight into the network quantization technique. 

2,
The paper evaluates the proposed method only on WMT14 En-De and En-Fr benchmark datasets. The effectiveness of the proposed method would be more convincing if it was evaluated on different datasets and tasks as well, e.g. wikitext-103 for language modeling.

3,
Not much insight and discussion are provided on why the proposed method works better than other baselines. For example, the ablation study offers very interesting observations, but the authors only state the fact, and not providing any hypotheses for further analyzing the reason of working well for the proposed method.

4,
One additional thing that I concern about this paper is the reproducibility of the experiments.
I could not find a detailed explanation of how the authors obtained the reported results written in the tables.
If the results were obtained from a single run for each method with the single random initialization, then it may be a bit unreliable.
It is because we often observe more than 1point BLEU difference in the same model configuration except for a random initialization.
To clear such suspicion, the authors should report the average BLEU of the several runs or release their code for reproducing their experiments in future validation.

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments.
As for your concerns:

Contrary to what you have mentioned, the main idea of this paper is not uniform quantization, it’s about quantization improving or not worsening translation quality. This is an important distinction as it is what we believe make this work novel. The Transformer paper is already two years old. If quantizing the architecture without impairing results was an easy task, papers would of had come out by then. The few papers released so far quantize much fewer components than we do and none of the proposed methods who quantize activations have managed to keep performance on par with full-precision. Considering all of this, we believe our work to be novel and impactful to the community.

In regards to your suggestions, we have added results on more translation datasets and on language modeling.

Finally, about your concern on reproducibility, we do not agree. Yes all translation experiments except post-quantization are single runs, but over the sheer number of experiments we ran, the trend is clear. In the case of 8-bit quantization for example, out of 41 experiments, 36 scored equal or higher BLEU than full-precision. We have added a mention in the paper about this. About code, it is in our intention to open-source it.

As with other reviewers, although disagreements, we are very thankful for your comments. These helped us shape a new and better paper. We hope our changes and clarifications will compel you to review your score. Thank you.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
This paper proposes a quantization strategy for Transformer models and demonstrate results on a neural machine translation benchmark. Although the results look promising, the experiments are a bit sparse in terms of details. In my opinion, an empirical performance-focused paper like this really needs to provide a lot of details. Specific recommendations:

- Table 1 compares BLEU scores across different papers. But is is not clear exactly whether they are comparable. In particular, what is the model size for the model in each paper? It would be insightful to show more details such as model size, compression rate, inference time, etc. 

- Table 2: the compression rate is shown as x4. But it would be good to show the actual model size as well. Some parameters, such as the bias terms, are not quantized, correct? 

- If you are also arguing that quantization gives inference time improvements, it would be good to show timing numbers too. I would recommend dedicate significant portion of the paper to this. 

- The ablation study is good. For empirical papers like this, these are the kind of analyses that will be particularly exciting to the reader in my opinion. So more analysis on different variants and practical strategies will be helpful. 

- I would cut all the pruning results (e.g. Sec 4.4). I don't see how that is related to quantization, which is the main contribution of the paper. The pruning results seem to be tacked on and make the paper a bit incoherent. 

- Finally, it is not very clear how does the proposed quantization method different from previous methods. The previous methods should be described with respect to your approach so it is easy to understand what is novel.

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments.
As for your concerns:

We did add more details in the experiments section, but more than that we feel would just be a repetition of what is already in the original Transformer paper or very unimportant information. Apart from a few mentioned exceptions, we used the exact same training setup as in their original paper.

About Table 1, we added model sizes and compression rate or lower bounds in cases when authors did not mention them. We also mentioned that all of these models are base Transformers and so their original uncompressed size is equivalent. Inference time were not given in any other papers.

We also added model sizes in Table 2.

As for your comment about inference time. We are not arguing that quantization gives inference time improvements because this is not something that needs to be argued. Computational efficiency gains is a by-product of quantization. By using fewer bits, we can perform more computations simultaneously on equivalent hardware.
Inference time is also a terrible metric for comparing methods, as this is highly hardware and implementation dependent. Reporting results such as: “our method performed X times faster than full-precision” is meaningless. Someone trying to replicate this could end up with completely different time gains. Dedicating a significant portion of the paper to this would be a total waste.

We’ve added more ablation studies to the paper.

We moved the pruning section to the appendix. We do not think it should be removed as the method is simple and improves compression. We firmly believe it is worth mentioning.

We’ve added more clarifications about how other methods differ from ours and hope this will help clear any confusion.

In light of our changes and clarifications, we hope you will reconsider your score. Thank you again for your comments. Although our disagreements, your comments definitely helped improve the paper and we are very grateful to you for this. Thank you.
